title: Public Sector Undertakings in India

{{short description|Government-owned entities in India}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2015}}
{{Use Indian English|date=December 2015}}
{{Politics of India}} 
'''Public Sector Undertakings''' ('''PSU''') in India are [[State-owned enterprise|government-owned entities]] in which at least 51% of stake is under the [[ownership]] of the [[Government of India]] or [[State governments of India|state governments]]. These types of firms can also be a joint venture of multiple PSUs. These entities perform commercial functions on behalf of the government.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Kaushik |first1=Kshama V. |last2=Dutta |first2=Kaushik |title=India Means Business |chapter=State-owned Enterprises or Public Sector Undertakings |date=2012 |chapter-url=https://academic.oup.com/book/10427/chapter-abstract/158255985 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |access-date=15 October 2023 |pages=86–106|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198072614.003.0004 |isbn=978-0-19-807261-4 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://164.100.47.194/loksabha/writereaddata/questions/Questions_Brochure.pdf |title=STATUTORY CORPORATIONS, COMPANIES AND OTHER BODIES IN WHICH THE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA HAVE FINANCIAL OR CONTROLLING INTEREST LOK SABHA SECRETARIAT|date=2021-09-01|work=Parliament of India, Lok Sabha}}</ref>
Depending on the level of government ownership, PSUs are officially classified into two categories: '''Central Public Sector Undertakings''' ('''CPSUs'''), owned by the central government or other CPSUs; and '''State  Public Sector Undertakings''' ('''SPSUs'''), owned by state governments. CPSU and SPSU is further classified into Strategic Sector and Non-Strategic Sector. Depending on their financial performance and progress, CPSUs are granted the status of Maharatna, Navaratna, and Miniratna (Category I and II).

Following [[India's independence]] in 1947, the limited pre-existing industries were insufficient for [[sustainable economic growth]]. The [[Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956]], adopted during the [[Five-Year Plans of India|Second Five-Year Plan]], laid the framework for PSUs. The government initially prioritized strategic sectors, such as communication, irrigation, chemicals, and [[heavy industries]], followed by the [[nationalisation]] of [[corporation]]s. PSUs subsequently expanded into consumer goods production and service areas like contracting, consulting, and transportation. Their goals include increasing exports, reducing imports, fostering infrastructure development, driving economic growth, and generating job opportunities. Each PSU has its own recruitment rules and employment in PSUs is highly sought after in India due to high pay and its [[job security]], with most preferring candidates with a [[Graduate Aptitude Test in Engineering|GATE]] score.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/education/careers/govt/psu-services/is-psu-a-government-job-public-sector-company-jobs-salary-more-/articleshow/94787399.cms | title=Is PSU a government job? Public Sector Company Jobs, Salary & more | newspaper=The Times of India | date=11 October 2022 }}</ref> These jobs are very well known for very high pay scale compared to other Government jobs such as UPSC, facilities such as [[bungalow]], [[pensions]] and other subsidized facility and for also very good [[planned city|planned townships]] settlement life. A PSU non-executives such as workers have a huge payscale difference compared to private sector.

In 1951, there were five PSUs under the ownership of the government. By March 2021, the number of such government entities had increased to 365.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Public Enterprises Survey 2019–20 {{!}} Department of Public Enterprises {{!}} MoHI&PE {{!}} GoI Page No. 1|url=https://dpe.gov.in/sites/default/files/PE_Survery_Vol_II_English_2019_20_0.pdf|website=dpe.gov.in|access-date=2020-05-31}}</ref> These government entities represented a total investment of about [[Indian rupee|₹]]16,410,000,000,000 as of 31 March 2019. Their total paid-up capital as of 31 March 2019 stood at about ₹200.76 lakh crore. CPSEs have earned a revenue of about ₹24,430,000,000,000 + ₹1,000,000,000,000  during the financial year 2018–19.<ref name=":0" />

==History==
{{further|Economic history of India}}
=== Soviet model ===
When India achieved independence in 1947, it was primarily an agrarian entity, with a weak industrial base. There were only eighteen state-owned [[Indian Ordnance Factories]], previously established to reduce the dependency of the [[British Indian Army]] on imported arms.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://ofb.gov.in/index.php?wh=history&lang=en |title = Home | Ordnance Factory Board | Government of India}}</ref>

The British Raj had previously elected to leave agricultural production to the [[Private sector]], with tea processing firms, jute mills (such as the [[Acland Mill]]), [[Rail transport in India#History|railways]], electricity utilities, banks, coal mines, and steel mills being just some of the economic entities largely owned by private individuals like the industrialist [[Jamsetji Tata]]. Other entities were listed on the [[Bombay Stock Exchange]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=[IRFCA] Indian Railways FAQ: IR History: Early Days - 1|url=https://www.irfca.org/faq/faq-hist.html|access-date=2021-05-15|website=www.irfca.org}}</ref>

Critics of private ownership of India's agricultural and industrial entities—most notably Mahatma Gandhi's independence movement—instead advocated for a self-sufficient, largely agrarian, communal village-based existence for India in the first half of the 20th century.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mahatma Gandhi believed in a self-sufficient village economy |url=https://www.mkgandhi.org/articles/bhuimali.php#:~:text=Gandhi%20is%20in%20favour%20of,soil%20and%20pollute%20the%20environment. |website=mkgandhi.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gosalia|first=Sushila|date=1979-03-01|title=The Gandhian model of self-reliance in the Indian economy|journal=Intereconomics|language=en|volume=14|issue=2|pages=80–83|doi=10.1007/BF02930202|issn=1613-964X|hdl-access=free|hdl=10419/139599|s2cid=56358907}}</ref> Other contemporary criticisms of India's public sector targeted the lack of well-funded schools, public libraries, universities, hospitals and medical and engineering colleges; a lack seen as impeding an Indian replication of Britain's own industrialization in the previous century.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Mushtaq|first=Muhammad Umair|date=January 2009|title=Public Health in British India: A Brief Account of the History of Medical Services and Disease Prevention in Colonial India|journal=Indian Journal of Community Medicine|volume=34|issue=1|pages=6–14|doi=10.4103/0970-0218.45369|issn=0970-0218|pmc=2763662|pmid=19876448 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Amrith|first=Sunil S.|date=Feb 2009|title=Health in India Since Independence|url=https://hummedia.manchester.ac.uk/institutes/gdi/publications/workingpapers/bwpi/bwpi-wp-7909.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Chaudhary|first=Latika|date=March 2009|title=Determinants of Primary Schooling in British India|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0022050709000400/type/journal_article|journal=The Journal of Economic History|language=en|volume=69|issue=1|pages=269–302|doi=10.1017/S0022050709000400|issn=0022-0507|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite SSRN |last=Chaudhary|first=Latika|date=2012-05-01|title=Caste, Colonialism and Schooling: Education in British India |language=en |ssrn=2087140}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Odgers |first=George Allen |date=October 1925 |title=Education in British India |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_phi-delta-kappan_1925-10_8_2/page/n1 |journal=The Phi Delta Kappan |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=1–6 |jstor=20257440 |jstor-access=free}}</ref>

Post-Independence, the national consensus turned in favor of rapid industrialisation of the economy, a process seen as the key to economic development, improved living standards and economic sovereignty.<ref name="Eaindustry">{{cite web | url=http://eaindustry.nic.in/handbk/chap001.pdf | title=Chapter 1, Industrial Policy Handbook | publisher=Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry | work=Industrial Policy Handbook | access-date=17 September 2015 | page=2 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528135133/http://eaindustry.nic.in/handbk/chap001.pdf | archive-date=28 May 2015 | df=dmy-all }}</ref> Building upon the [[Bombay Plan]], which noted the necessity of government intervention and regulation in the economy, the first Industrial Policy Resolution announced in 1948 laid down in broad strokes such a strategy of industrial development. Later, the [[Planning Commission (India)|Planning Commission]] was formed by a cabinet resolution in March 1950 and the Industrial (Development and Regulation) Act was enacted in 1951 with the objective of empowering the government to take necessary steps to regulate industry.<ref name="Jadhav">{{cite web | url=http://www.drnarendrajadhav.info/drnjadhav_web_files/Published%20papers/Indian%20Industrial%20Policy%20Since%201956.pdf | title=Industrial Policy since 1956 | publisher=Dr. Narendra Jadhav | access-date=17 September 2015 | author=Jadhav, Narendra}}</ref>

The first [[Prime Minister of India|Prime Minister]] of India, [[Jawaharlal Nehru]], promoted an economic policy based on [[import substitution industrialisation]] and advocated a [[mixed economy]].<ref name="Ghosh">{{cite book | title=Jawaharlal Nehru | publisher=Allied Publishers | author=Ghose, Shankar | year=1993 | page=243 | isbn=978-81-7023-369-5}}</ref> He believed that the establishment of basic and heavy industry was fundamental to the development and modernisation of the Indian economy. India's second [[Five-Year Plans of India|five year plan]] (1956–60) and the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 emphasized the development of public sector enterprises to meet Nehru's national [[industrialisation]] policy. His vision was carried forward by [[V. Krishnamurthy]], a figure known as the "Father of Public sector undertakings in India". Indian statistician [[Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis]] was instrumental to its formulation, which was later termed the [[Feldman–Mahalanobis model]].<ref name="Ahluwalia">{{cite book | title=Productivity and Growth in Indian Manufacturing, ''part of'' Recent Developments in Indian Economy: With Special Reference to Structural Reforms, Part 2 | publisher=Academic Foundation | author=Ahluwalia, Isher J. |year=1993 | location=New Delhi | page=25 | isbn=978-81-7188-094-2}}</ref><ref name="Nayar">Baldev Raj Nayar, Globalization And Nationalism: The Changing Balance Of India's Economic Policy, 1950–2000 (New Delhi: Sage, 2001)</ref>

In 1969, [[Indira Gandhi]]'s government [[nationalisation|nationalised]] fourteen of India's largest private banks, and an additional six in 1980. This government-led industrial policy, with corresponding restrictions on private enterprise, was the dominant pattern of Indian economic development until the [[1991 Indian economic crisis]].<ref name="Jadhav" /> After the crisis, the government began [[divestment|divesting]] its ownership of several PSUs to raise capital and privatize companies facing poor financial performance and low efficiency.<ref name="BSEPSU">{{cite web | url=http://www.bsepsu.com/historical-disinvestment.asp | title=Disinvestments-A Historical Perspective | publisher=[[Bombay Stock Exchange]] | access-date=19 September 2015}}</ref><ref name="Divestment">{{cite journal | title=Divestments in Public Enterprises: The Indian Experience |author=Sankar, T.L. |author2=Mishra, R.K. |author3=Lateef Syed Mohammed, A. | journal= International Journal of Public Sector Management| year=1994 | volume=7 | issue=2 | pages=69–88 | doi=10.1108/09513559410055242}}</ref>

=== Rise of Dirigisme after 1991 reforms===
After [[Economic liberalisation in India|liberalisation]] in 1991, India shifted from a mixed [[Five-year plans of the Soviet Union|planned]] led [[Sovietization|Soviet model]] to a more market-oriented ''[[Dirigisme|dirigisme]]'' economy with [[Indicative planning|indicative planning]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/Statistical_year_book_india_chapters/ch7.pdf |format=PDF|title=Chapter-7 : FIVE YEAR PLANS|website=Mospi.gov.in|access-date=22 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="FP">{{cite news|last1=Babones|first1=Salvatore|date=27 July 2011|title=Why France Has a Much Better India Strategy Than America|work=FP|url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2021/02/01/france-india-better-strategy-than-america/}}</ref><ref name="GOVERNANCENOW">{{cite news|last1=Srivastava|first1=Pankaj|date=27 July 2011|title=I believe the neoliberal regime is also reaching a dead end: Prabhat Patnaik|work=GOVERNANCENOW|url=https://www.governancenow.com/views/interview/i-believe-the-neoliberal-regime-also-reaching-a-dead-end-prabhat-patnaik}}</ref> 
The 1991 reforms led to formation of [[state sector|pseudo-state]] owned companies by [[Government of India]] such as [[National Stock Exchange of India|NSE]], [[National Securities Depository Limited|NSDL]], [[CRISIL]], [[Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services|IL&FS]], [[Infrastructure Development Finance Company|IDFC]] etc. which were joint-venture of Public Sector Undertakings(PSUs) and controlling stake(>25%) owned by PSUs as a [[Protectionism|protectionist policy]] to lead the market reforms instead of invisible free-hand of free market.The Eighth Five Year Plan (1992 - 1997) adopted Indicative Planning in India. The Eighth Five Year Plan (1992 - 1997) managed the transition from a centrally planned economy to a market led economy through indicative planning and [[public sector]].According to government data, 96 new CPSEs were incorporated between 2014 and 2022.<ref>https://www.outlookbusiness.com/news/government-incorporated-96-new-cpses-since-2014-data-news-191905</ref>

==Management and classification==
The public sector undertakings are headed by the head of board of directors also known as ''chairperson cum managing director cum chief executive officer'' and a ''vice chairperson cum deputy managing director cum co-chief executive officer'' along with the members of the  board of directors also known as ''executive director cum c-level officer'' who are Group 'A' gazetted officers appointed by the [[President of India]] in case of central public sector undertakings, its subsidiaries & its divisions and appointed by the [[Governor (India)|Governor of States of India]] in case of state public sector undertakings, its subsidiaries & its divisions.

All of the public sector undertakings have been awarded additional financial autonomy. ''Public Sector Undertakings'' are [[Government|government establishment]]s that have comparative advantages", giving them greater autonomy to compete in the global market so as to "support [them] in their drive to become global giants".<ref name="announcement">[http://dpe.nic.in/nm1.htm Original govt. announcement about the Navratnas 1997] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120209171125/http://dpe.nic.in/nm1.htm |date=9 February 2012 }}</ref> Financial autonomy was initially awarded to nine PSUs as ''Navratna'' status in 1997.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rediff.com/money/slide-show/slide-show-1-the-maharatnas-navratnas-of-india/20100826.htm|title=Maharatnas, Navratnas: India's best PSUs!|website=Rediff}}</ref> Originally, the term ''[[Navaratna]]'' meant a talisman composed of nine precious gems. Later, this term was adopted in the courts of the Gupta emperor [[Vikramaditya]] and Mughal emperor [[Akbar]], as the collective name for [[Navaratnas|nine extraordinary courtiers]] at their respective courts.

In 2010, the central government established the higher ''Maharatna'' category, which raises a public sector unit's investment ceiling from ₹1,000 crore to ₹5,000 crores.<ref name="maharatna09">{{cite news|title=Maharatna status for mega PSUs gets nod|work=The Times of India|url=http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/biz/india-business/Maharatna-status-for-mega-PSUs-gets-nod/articleshow/5375541.cms|date=25 December 2009|access-date=29 December 2009}}</ref> The ''Maharatna'' public sector units can now decide on investments of up to 15 per cent of their net worth in a project while the ''Navaratna'' companies could invest up to ₹1,000 crore without explicit government approval. Two categories of ''Miniratnas'' afford less extensive financial autonomy.

PSUs in India are also categorized based on their special non-financial objectives and are registered under Section 8 of [[Companies Act 2013|Companies Act]], 2013 (erstwhile Section 25 of Companies Act, 1956).

==List of CPSUs==
{{main|List of public sector undertakings in India}}

Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) can be classified as Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs) or State Public Sector Undertakings (SPSUs). CPSUs are administered by the [[Ministry of Heavy Industries]]. The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), [[Ministry of Finance (India)|Ministry of Finance]] is the nodal department for all the Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs).

As of 2025, there are 14 Maharatnas, 26 Navratnas and 65 Miniratnas (divided into Category 1 and Category 2).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.jagranjosh.com/general-knowledge/list-of-maharatna-and-navratna-companies-in-india-1467721897-1 |title=List of Maharatna and Navratna companies in India |work=Dainik Jagran |date=8 April 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=http://dpe.gov.in/about-us/management-division/list-maharatna-navratna-and-miniratna-cpses |title=List of Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna CPSEs |work=Ministry of Finance |access-date=24 September 2021 }}</ref>

extract:
Public Sector Undertakings (PSU) in India are government-owned entities in which at least 51% of stake is under the ownership of the Government of India or state governments. These types of firms can also be a joint venture of multiple PSUs. These entities perform commercial functions on behalf of the government.
Depending on the level of government ownership, PSUs are officially classified into two categories: Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), owned by the central government or other CPSUs; and State  Public Sector Undertakings (SPSUs), owned by state governments. CPSU and SPSU is further classified into Strategic Sector and Non-Strategic Sector. Depending on their financial performance and progress, CPSUs are granted the status of Maharatna, Navaratna, and Miniratna (Category I and II).
Following India's independence in 1947, the limited pre-existing industries were insufficient for sustainable economic growth. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956, adopted during the Second Five-Year Plan, laid the framework for PSUs. The government initially prioritized strategic sectors, such as communication, irrigation, chemicals, and heavy industries, followed by the nationalisation of corporations. PSUs subsequently expanded into consumer goods production and service areas like contracting, consulting, and transportation. Their goals include increasing exports, reducing imports, fostering infrastructure development, driving economic growth, and generating job opportunities. Each PSU has its own recruitment rules and employment in PSUs is highly sought after in India due to high pay and its job security, with most preferring candidates with a GATE score. These jobs are very well known for very high pay scale compared to other Government jobs such as UPSC, facilities such as bungalow, pensions and other subsidized facility and for also very good planned townships settlement life. A PSU non-executives such as workers have a huge payscale difference compared to private sector.
In 1951, there were five PSUs under the ownership of the government. By March 2021, the number of such government entities had increased to 365. These government entities represented a total investment of about ₹16,410,000,000,000 as of 31 March 2019. Their total paid-up capital as of 31 March 2019 stood at about ₹200.76 lakh crore. CPSEs have earned a revenue of about ₹24,430,000,000,000 + ₹1,000,000,000,000  during the financial year 2018–19.
